Surah 25: al-Furqan (The Criterion). It is Meccan, and its number of verses is seventy-seven.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) upon His servant﴾. Its good increased greatly, from *barakah* (blessing), which is the abundance of good. Or [it means] He grew in excellence above everything and was exalted above it in His attributes and His acts, for *barakah* includes the meaning of increase. Its being mentioned in connection with His sending down *al-Furqan* is either because of the abundance of good in it, or because it indicates His exaltedness. It has also been said that *tabaraka* derives from *buruk al-tayr 'ala al-ma'* (birds settling on water), and from it comes *al-birkah* (pool), because the water remains in it. It is not to be made subject to any disposal and is not used except for Allah, exalted is He. *Al-Furqan* is a verbal noun from *faraqa bayna al-shay'ayn*, meaning he separated between two things when he divided them. The Qur'an is named by it because it separates truth from falsehood through its affirmation, or the one who is right from the one who is wrong through its inimitability, or because some of it is separated from other parts in its revelation. It was also recited as "upon His servants" (*'ibadihi*), meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his community, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses﴾. Or [it means] the prophets, on the basis that *al-Furqan* is a generic noun for the heavenly books.

﴿That it may be﴾: the servant or the Criterion. ﴿a warner to the worlds﴾: to the jinn and mankind. ﴿nadhiran﴾ means a warner, or a warning, like *al-nakir* in the sense of *al-inkar* (denial). This clause, although it is not something known, is treated as known because its evidence is strong, and it has been made a relative clause (*silah*).

﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a substitute for the first [attribute], or a laudatory [predicate] in the nominative or accusative. ﴿And He has not taken a son﴾, as the Christians claim. ﴿And He has no partner in the dominion﴾, as the dualists (*thanawiyyah*) say. He affirmed to Him dominion absolutely and negated whatever could stand in its place or oppose Him in it. Then He drew attention to what indicates this, saying: ﴿And He created everything﴾, He brought it into being in a manner that observed measure according to His will, such as His creating man from specific materials and in determined forms and shapes. ﴿And He determined it with determination﴾: He determined it and prepared it for what He willed from it of properties and functions, such as preparing man for perception, understanding, reflection, management, drawing out various crafts, and practicing diverse works, and so on. Or [it means] He determined it to remain until a specified term. The word *khalq* (creation) is sometimes used for mere bringing into existence without regard to its derivation, so the meaning would be: He brought every thing into existence and determined it in its bringing into being, so that it would not be disproportionate.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 7–8:

﴿And they say: "What is wrong with this Messenger?"﴾ That is, "What is the matter with this one who claims to be a messenger?" There is in this contempt (istihanah) and mockery (tahakkum). ﴿He eats food﴾ as we eat.

﴿And walks in the markets﴾ seeking livelihood as we walk. The meaning is: if his claim is true, then why does his condition not differ from our condition? This is due to their bewilderment (amah) and the limitation of their vision to sensible things (mahsusat), for the distinction of the messengers from others is not by corporeal matters but by inner states (ahwal nafsaniyyah), as God, exalted is He, indicated by His saying: ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me that your God is one God﴾. ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him so that he would be a warner with him?﴾ so that we might know his truthfulness through the angel's confirmation of him.

﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him﴾ so that he would be sufficiently supported by it and would be free from seeking livelihood. ﴿Or he have a garden from which he eats﴾. This is by way of descent (al-tanazzul), i.e., if no treasure is thrown down to him, then at least he should have a garden like that of the landowners (al-dahaqin) and the well-to-do (al-mayasir), so that he may live off its produce. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿nakulu﴾ with the nun, and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers.

﴿And the wrongdoers said﴾: the wrongdoers (al-zalimun) is placed in the position of their pronoun, as a recording against them of wrongdoing in what they said. ﴿You follow only﴾ what you follow. ﴿Except a man bewitched (mashur)﴾: he was bewitched (suhira) so that his mind was overcome, and it was said: one who has a sihr, which is the windpipe (al-ri'ah), i.e., a human being and not an angel.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 9–10:

﴿Look how they have coined comparisons for you﴾, that is: they uttered about you bizarre statements and invented for you strange conditions. ﴿So they have gone astray﴾ from the path that leads to recognising the distinctive qualities of the Prophet and distinguishing him from the false claimant to prophethood (al-mutanabbi), so they stumble about like one who is blind-sided (khabt 'ashwa'). ﴿So they cannot find a way﴾ to discredit your prophethood, or to right guidance and direction.(p-119)

﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, shall give you﴾ in this world ﴿better than that﴾ which they have said, but He has deferred it to the Hereafter, because it is better and more lasting. ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ is a substitution (badal) for ﴿better﴾. ﴿And He shall give you palaces﴾ is conjoined (ʿutifa) upon the position (mahall) of the conditional clause. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read it in the nominative (raf'), because when the conditional verb is in the past tense, its response may be either in the jussive (jazm) or the nominative (raf'), as in the verse of the poet:

"And if a friend comes to him on a day of hunger... he says: 'My wealth is not absent, nor is my family [i.e., I have no lack]'"

It is also permissible that it be a resumed statement (isti'naf), promising what he will have in the Hereafter. It has also been read in the accusative (nasb), on the basis that it is a response introduced by the conjunction "wa" (waw).

Nay, they denied the Hour. Their outlook was confined to the trivial goods of this world, and they thought that honour lies only in wealth. So they slandered you for your poverty. Or, for that reason, they denied you, not for the corrupt slanders they contrived. Or, how could they turn to this answer and believe you about what God has promised you in the Hereafter? Or, do not be surprised at their denial of you, for it is more surprising than that.

And We have prepared for him who denies the Hour a blaze: a fire of intense flaring. It is also said that "saʿīr" is a name for Jahannam (Hell), in which case its not taking the full declension is by consideration of it as a place-name.

When it sees them from afar: this means when it is in their sight, as in the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying, "Their fires should not be in sight of each other" (lā tatarāʾā nārāhumā), meaning that they should not be so close that one of them is within sight of the other. This is figurative usage (majāz), and the feminine form is used because it refers to the fire or to Jahannam. From a far distance: this is the furthest distance from which it can be seen.

They hear from it a roaring of rage and a wheezing: the sound of rage. It likens the sound of its boiling to the sound of one who is enraged, and to his wheezing, which is a sound heard from the chest. Moreover, since life is not, in our view, conditional upon bodily structure, it is possible that God creates life in it, so that it sees, rages and wheezes. It is also said that this belongs to its guardians (zabāniyah), and it is attributed to it by omitting the modifier (ḥadhf al-muḍāf).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 15–16:

﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised?"﴾ The demonstrative refers to the punishment. The interrogation (istifham), the preference (tafdil), and the alternation (taraddud) are for rebuke (taqri') together with mockery (tahakkum). Alternatively, it refers to the ( كَنْزٌ ) (treasure) and the ( جَنَّةُ ) (garden). The returning pronoun to the relative clause is omitted. The idafa of ( جَنَّةُ ) to ( الخُلْدِ ) (eternity) is for praise, or to indicate its everlastingness, or to distinguish it from the gardens of this world. ﴿Which is for them﴾ in the knowledge of God, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh), or because what God has promised is as though it has already occurred in its certainty. ﴿A reward﴾ for their deeds, by the promise. ﴿And a destination﴾ to which they return. That it is a reward for them does not prevent Him from bestowing it upon others as a favour, by their consent, while it is also permissible that by "the God-fearing" is meant those who guard against disbelief and denial, because they are in contrast to them.

﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾: whatever they wish of bliss. Perhaps the aspirations of each group are limited to what befits its rank, since it is apparent that the lesser cannot attain the reach of the perfect by mere desire. In this there is a reminder that all desires are fulfilled only in the Garden.

﴿Abiding forever﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from one of their pronouns. ﴿It is ever a promise, one to be asked for﴾: the pronoun in ( كانَ ) (was) refers to ( ما يَشاءُونَ ) (what they wish), and "the promise" means the promised thing, i.e., that thing was promised and worthy of being asked for and requested. Or it means "one to be asked for," which people request in their supplication: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. Or it refers to the angels, in their words: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them into the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them﴾. The sense of obligation (wujub) in ( عَلى ) (upon) is because God's promise cannot be broken, and this does not entail that He is compelled to fulfil it, since the will's attachment to the promises precedes the promise that necessitates fulfilment.

﴿Abiding forever﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from one of their pronouns. ﴿It is ever a promise, one to be asked for﴾: the pronoun in ( كانَ ) (was) refers to ( ما يَشاءُونَ ) (what they wish), and "the promise" means the promised thing, i.e., that thing was promised and worthy of being asked for and requested. Or it means "one to be asked for," which people request in their supplication: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. Or it refers to the angels, in their words: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them into the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them﴾. The sense of obligation (wujub) in ( عَلى ) (upon) is because God's promise cannot be broken, and this does not entail that He is compelled to fulfil it, since the will's attachment to the promises precedes the promise that necessitates fulfilment.

(And on the Day when We gather them) for recompense. It is also read with a kasra on the shin (نَحْشُرُهم → nahshiruhum / نَحْشِرُهم), and Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub and Hafs read it with the ya' (يَحْشُرُهم, "He gathers them"). ﴿And what they worshipped besides Allah﴾ encompasses every object of worship other than Him, the Exalted. The use of "ma" (ما, "what") is either because its original application is more general, which is why it is applied to every shape that is seen but not recognized; or because it is used to mean an attribute, as if it were said "and their object of worship"; or by way of giving precedence to the idols, to belittle them, or by considering the majority of its worshippers; or it is specific to the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah, by the indication of the question and answer; or it refers to the idols, which Allah causes to speak, or which speak through the tongue of their state, as it has been said regarding the speech of hands and feet. ﴿Then He will say﴾, that is, to the objects of worship, and this is a shift in address (taluwin al-khitab). It is a question of rebuke and reproach directed at the worshippers. Its underlying form is (أأضللتم) "did you lead astray" ... (ضلوا) "or did they stray", and the word order was changed so that the interrogative particle, which is the object of the question, comes first, and it is the one that governs the verb rather than the other way around, because there is no doubt about it; otherwise the reproach would not be directed. And the complement of the verb "ḍalla" (to stray) is omitted for emphasis (mubalagha).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 18–19:

﴿They said: "Glory be to You!"﴾ in amazement at what was said to them, because they are either angels or infallible prophets, or inanimate objects that have no power over anything. Or it is an indication that they are the ones described with glorifying Him and affirming His oneness, so how would it befit them to lead His servants astray? Or it is a declaration of God Most High's transcendence above rivals.

﴿It was not for us﴾ meaning: it would not be valid for us. ﴿to take any protectors besides You﴾ either because of infallibility or because of lack of power. So how could it be valid for us to call others than ourselves to take up any guardian besides You? It is read (nuttakhadha) in the passive voice, from (ittakhadha), which takes two objects, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God took Abraham as an intimate friend﴾. Its second object is (min awliya') ["any protectors"], and (min) here is partitive; on the first reading it is superfluous, for emphasis of the negation.

﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment﴾ with various kinds of blessings, so they became absorbed in desires. ﴿until they forgot the Reminder﴾ until they became heedless of Your remembrance, or of reflecting on Your bounties and pondering Your signs. This attributes the misguidance to them insofar as it arises from their own acquisition, and also ascribes it to what God did to them, by which He caused them to be so; this is exactly what we have maintained, so it does not stand as an argument against us from the Mu'tazilites.

﴿And they were﴾ in Your decree ﴿a people doomed﴾, destroyed. It is a verbal noun described by the adjective, which is why it is the same for singular and plural; or it is the plural of (ba'ir), like (a'idh) and ('udh).

﴿So they have indeed denied you﴾: a turn (iltifat) toward the worshippers, by way of argument and obligation, with the verb "say" omitted; the meaning is: "So the ones worshipped have denied you"﴿by what you say﴾ in your claim that they are gods, or that "these led us astray." The bi' here means "in," or it is with the genitive as a substitute for the pronoun. According to Ibn Kathir, it is read with the yā' (yukadhdhibukum), meaning: ﴿they denied you﴾ by their saying ﴿Glory be to You! It was not for us...﴾.

﴿So they cannot avert﴾ (fa-ma yastati'un), i.e., the ones worshipped. Hafs read it with the tā' (tastati'un), addressing the worshippers. ﴿nor any help﴾: ﴿averting﴾ means repelling punishment from you; it is also said to mean a stratagem, from their saying "innahu la-yatasarraf," meaning he devises a scheme. ﴿Nor help﴾ means one who would assist you against it.

﴿And whoever among you wrongs﴾, O accountable ones, ﴿We will make him taste a great punishment﴾. This is the Fire. The condition, though general and covering everyone who disbelieves or commits grave sin, is by consensus restricted in its requirement of recompense by the absence of a preventing factor, which is repentance; and by the consensus that obedience nullifies it, and according to us, by pardon.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 20:

﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they surely ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ That is, "except messengers who..." (illa rusulan innahum). The described noun (mawsuf) is omitted, since the word "messengers" (al-mursalin) indicates it, and the descriptive phrase (sifah) is put in its place, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal), in which only the pronoun is retained; and this is a response to their saying: ﴿What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?﴾

It is also read as "yumashsha'un" (they are made to walk), meaning: their needs make them walk, or people make them walk. ﴿And We have made some of you﴾, O people, ﴿a trial for others﴾, a test. This is a consolation to the Messenger of God ﷺ regarding what they said after his violation (of their expectations). In it is evidence for qadar (divine decree) and destiny. ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ is a cause for the making (of the trial), and the meaning is: "We made some of you a trial for others so that We may know which of you will be patient." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 21:

﴿And those who do not hope﴾ (lā yarjūna): do not expect (lā yamlūna). ﴿for Our meeting﴾ (liqā'anā) with good, because of their disbelief in the Resurrection; or, they do not fear Our meeting with evil, according to the dialect of Tihama. The root meaning of liqā' (encounter) is arrival at a thing, and from it comes ru'yah (seeing), for it is arrival at the thing seen. What is intended here is arrival at its recompense. It is also possible that ru'yah (seeing) is intended according to the first interpretation. ﴿Why not?﴾ (lawlā): hallā (why not). ﴿Were angels sent down to us﴾ (unzila 'alaynā al-malā'ikah), so that they would inform us of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: so that they would be messengers to us. ﴿Or should we see our Lord﴾ (aw nara rabbanā), so that He would command us to affirm him and follow him. ﴿They have certainly become arrogant within themselves﴾ (laqadi istakbarū fī anfusihim), meaning: concerning their own selves, to the point that they desired for themselves what befell certain individuals among the prophets, who are the most perfect of God's creation, at their most perfect times, and what is greater than that. ﴿And they have transgressed﴾ (wa 'ataw): and exceeded the limit in wrongdoing. ﴿with a great transgression﴾ (utuwwan kabīrā): reaching the furthest of its degrees, since they witnessed overwhelming miracles yet turned away from them, and proposed for their wicked selves what the lofty aspirations of holy souls are barred from. The lām (in laqad) is the answer to an omitted oath, and beginning the sentence with a nominal clause is elegant and conveys a sense of wonder at their arrogance and their transgression, like his saying:

Ja'ratu Jassās abba'nā bi-nābihā... Kulaybān 'alat nāba Kulaybin bawā'uhā

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 25, verses 22–23**

﴿On the Day they see the angels﴾: the angels of death or the angels of punishment. "The Day" (*yawma*) is governed by *udhkur* ("remember") or by what it indicates. ﴿There will be no glad tidings that Day for the guilty﴾. Here *fa-innahu* carries the sense of "they are prevented from glad tidings" or "they are deprived of it." *Yawma'idhin* ("that Day") is either a repetition (*takrir*) or a predicate (*khabar*). *Lil-mujrimin* ("for the guilty") is either an explanation (*tabyin*), a second predicate, or an adverbial complement (*zarf*) for what the preposition *lam* depends on. It may also depend on *bushra* ("glad tidings") if *bushra* is read as indefinite and nunated, not built, with *la* ("no"), since in that case *la* does not govern it. *Lil-mujrimin* may be general, so that its ruling covers them by way of proof, and the negation of glad tidings for the guilty in general at that time does not entail the negation of glad tidings through pardon and intercession at another time. Or it may be specific, placed in the position of their pronoun to record their crime and to indicate what prevents glad tidings and what necessitates their opposite.

﴿And they say: a barrier, a forbidden barrier﴾: this is conjoined (*ʿutifa*) to what is implied, meaning: and the disbelievers will say this at that time. The phrase is a seeking of refuge and a request to God, exalted is He, that He prevent their meeting. It is one of the things they used to say upon meeting an enemy or encountering something hateful. Or the angels say it, meaning: forbidden, prohibited for you is Paradise or glad tidings. *Hujran* is also read with a *damma* (*hujran*). Its original form is with a *fatha*, but since it became restricted to a particular position, it was altered, like *qaʿdika* and *ʿumurika*. For this reason it is not inflected and its governing verb does not appear. He described it as *mahjuran* for emphasis, as in their saying: *mawtun ma'it* ("a dying death").

﴿And We turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾: meaning, We intend (*ʿamadna*) what they did in their disbelief of noble deeds, such as hospitality to guests, maintaining family ties, and relieving the distressed. So We nullified it, because the condition that makes it count was absent. This is a comparison of their state and deeds with the state of a people who disobeyed their ruler, whereupon he turned to their possessions, tore them apart, nullified them, and left no trace of them. *Habaʾan* is the dust seen in a ray of light entering through a window, from *habwa*, which is dust. *Mansuran* is its attribute. He likened their nullified deeds to *habaʾ* in its worthlessness and uselessness, then to what is scattered from it in its dispersal, such that it cannot be gathered or directed toward the aims they used to pursue. Or it is a third object (*maf'ul thalith*) in that it is like a predicate after a predicate, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 25–26:

﴿And the day the sky is split asunder﴾ Its original form is tatashaqqaqu (تتشقق), and the ta' was elided. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn Amir and Ya'qub assimilated it (idghams it) into the following letter.

﴿with the clouds﴾ Because of the emergence of clouds from it, namely the clouds mentioned in His words: ﴿Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾ And ﴿the angels will be sent down with a grand descent﴾, in those clouds, bearing the records of the deeds of the servants. Ibn Kathir recited «wa-nunazzilu» (we will send down). It is also read «wa-nuzzilat» and «wa-anzala» and «wa-nuzzila al-mala'ikatu», with the nun of the word elided.

﴿Sovereignty on that Day belongs truly to the All-Merciful﴾ The true sovereignty that is established for Him, because every other sovereignty will be annulled on that Day and only His sovereignty will remain. Thus the predicate is (al-haqq), and (lil-Rahman) is its complement; or it is an explanation. (Yawma'idhin) is the object of (al-mulk) and not of (al-haqq), because it comes later; or it is its adjective, and the predicate is (yawma'idhin) or (lil-Rahman). ﴿And it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾, severe.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 27–29:

﴿And on the Day when the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾ out of the intensity of regret. Biting the hands, eating the fingertips, gnashing the teeth and similar acts are metaphors (kinayat) for rage and regret, because they are among their accompaniments. By "the wrongdoer" (al-zalim) is meant the category (al-jins).

It has been said: "ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt used to frequently sit with the Prophet ﷺ. He invited him to his hospitality, but he refused to eat of his food until he pronounced the two testimonies (al-shahadatayn). He did so. Ubayy ibn Khalaf was his friend, and he rebuked him and said, 'You have apostatized (sabaʾta)!' He said, 'No, but I swore that he would not eat of my food while he was in my house, so I was ashamed before him (fa-istahyaytu minhu) (p-123) and testified for him.' Ubayy said, 'I will not be satisfied with you unless you go to him, step on his neck and spit in his face.' So he found him prostrating in Dar al-Nadwa and did that. The Prophet ﷺ, upon him be peace, said, 'I will not meet you outside Makkah except that I will strike your head with the sword.' So he was taken captive on the Day of Badr, and he ordered ʿAli to kill him, and he killed him. And he stabbed Ubayy at Uhud in single combat, and he returned to Makkah and died.''

﴿He will say: "Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger."﴾ A path to salvation, or one single path, namely the path of truth, and the paths of misguidance had not divided me.

﴿"Woe to me!"﴾ It is also read with the yā' (ya-wayla-ti) according to the original form. ﴿"I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend."﴾ He means whoever led him astray. "So-and-so" (fulan) is a metaphor for proper names, just as "hunā" here is a metaphor for categories.

﴿"He has indeed led me astray from the Reminder"﴾ from the remembrance of God, or His Book, or the admonition of the Messenger, or the word of testimony. ﴿"after it had come to me"﴾ and I had become firmly established in it. ﴿"And Satan is ever a deserter to man."﴾ He means the misguiding close friend, or Iblis, because he drove him to his friendship and to opposing the Messenger, or anyone among jinn and humans who acts like a devil. ﴿"a deserter to man"﴾ he befriends him until he brings him to ruin, then abandons him and does not benefit him; fa'ul is from al-khidhlan (forsaking).

He invited him to his hospitality, but he refused to eat of his food until he pronounced the two testimonies (al-shahadatayn). He did so. Ubayy ibn Khalaf was his friend, and he rebuked him and said, 'You have apostatized (sabaʾta)!' He said, 'No, but I swore that he would not eat of my food while he was in my house, so I was ashamed before him (fa-istahyaytu minhu) (p-123) and testified for him.' Ubayy said, 'I will not be satisfied with you unless you go to him, step on his neck and spit in his face.' So he found him prostrating in Dar al-Nadwa and did that. The Prophet ﷺ, upon him be peace, said, 'I will not meet you outside Makkah except that I will strike your head with the sword.' So he was taken captive on the Day of Badr, and he ordered ʿAli to kill him, and he killed him. And he stabbed Ubayy at Uhud in single combat, and he returned to Makkah and died.''

﴿He will say: "Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger."﴾ A path to salvation, or one single path, namely the path of truth, and the paths of misguidance had not divided me.

﴿"Woe to me!"﴾ It is also read with the yā' (ya-wayla-ti) according to the original form. ﴿"I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend."﴾ He means whoever led him astray. "So-and-so" (fulan) is a metaphor for proper names, just as "hunā" here is a metaphor for categories.

﴿"He has indeed led me astray from the Reminder"﴾ from the remembrance of God, or His Book, or the admonition of the Messenger, or the word of testimony. ﴿"after it had come to me"﴾ and I had become firmly established in it. ﴿"And Satan is ever a deserter to man."﴾ He means the misguiding close friend, or Iblis, because he drove him to his friendship and to opposing the Messenger, or anyone among jinn and humans who acts like a devil. ﴿"a deserter to man"﴾ he befriends him until he brings him to ruin, then abandons him and does not benefit him; fa'ul is from al-khidhlan (forsaking).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 30–31:

﴿And the Messenger says﴾: Muhammad, on that Day, or in the world, complaining (*bathth*) to God, Exalted is He. ﴿"My Lord, my people﴾: the Quraysh. ﴿have taken this Qur'an as abandoned (*mahjur*)﴾: by leaving it and turning people away from it. It is related from him, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever learns the Qur'an, hangs his *mushaf* (the written copy of the Qur'an) and does not attend to it or look into it, will come on the Day of Resurrection clinging to it, saying: 'My Lord, this servant of Yours has taken me as abandoned; judge between me and him.'"

Or they abandoned it and engaged in idle talk about it when they heard it, or they claimed that it was idle talk and "the fables of the ancients." Then its original form would be *mahjuran fihi* (abandoned concerning it), and the preposition was deleted. It is also permissible that *mahjur* carries the meaning of the verbal noun *hajr* (abandonment), like *majlud* and *ma'qul*. In this there is a warning to his people, for when the prophets, peace be upon them, complained to God, Exalted is He, about their people, He hastened punishment for them.

﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, just as We appointed one for you. So be patient, as they were patient. In this is evidence that He is the Creator of evil. The word *'aduww* (enemy) may refer to the singular and the plural. ﴿And your Lord suffices as a guide﴾ to the path of their subjugation. ﴿And as a helper﴾ for you against them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 32:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾ That is, it was sent down to him as a report, in the sense of "he was informed," so that it would not contradict His saying: ﴿All at once, in a single installment﴾ (jumlatan wahidatan), that is, in one go, like the three Books (al-kutub al-thalatha). This is an objection with no substance, because the inimitability (i'jaz) does not differ whether it is sent down all at once or in parts, although there are benefits (fawa'id) to gradual revelation (al-tafriq). Among them is what He indicated by His saying: ﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾, that is, thus did We send it down in parts, so that by its being divided We might strengthen your heart to memorize it and understand it. This is because his situation differs from the situations of Musa, Dawud and Isa, for he, upon him be blessings and peace, was unlettered (ummiyyan), whereas they used to write. Had it been cast upon him all at once, he would have been burdened in memorizing it, and perhaps it would not have been firmly established for him, for receiving (al-talaqqur) can only be achieved bit by bit. Also, its descent in accordance with events necessitates greater insight and deeper penetration into its meaning. Also, when it descended in installments, and he was challenged with each installment, and they were unable to produce its equal, that increased the strength of his heart. Also, when Jibril brought it to him stage after stage, it strengthened his heart. Among the benefits is knowledge of the abrogating (al-nasikh) and the abrogated (al-mansukh). Among them is the combination of contextual indications (al-qara'in al-haliyya) with verbal indications (al-dalalat al-lafziyya), for this aids eloquence (al-balagha). Likewise is the description of an omitted verbal noun (masdar mahdhuf), and the indication to its being sent down in parts, for it is implied by His saying: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾. It is possible that it is part of the speech of the disbelievers, and for this reason it is pausing point upon it, so it would be a circumstantial clause (hal). The indication to the previous Books and the lam in both cases is related to an omitted element.

﴿And We have recited it in measured recitation (tartilan)﴾, and We have read it to you, one thing after another, with deliberation and deliberateness, over twenty years or twenty-three years. The original meaning of tartil is in the teeth (al-asnan), and it is their being spaced apart (tafliju-ha).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 25, verses 33–34:

﴿And they will not bring you any comparison﴾: an astonishing question, as if it were a proverb of falsehood, by which they intend to discredit your prophethood. ﴿Except that We bring you the truth﴾ that overturns it in its answer. ﴿And better in explanation﴾: and something better in clarification or in meaning than their question. Or: they will not bring you a strange state, saying, "Why was his state not like this?" Except that We give you, of the states, what befits you in Our wisdom, and what is better in disclosing that for which you were sent.

﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell﴾: that is, turned upside down, or dragged upon it, or their hearts attached to lowly things, their faces turned toward it. It is related from him, upon him be prayers and peace: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three categories: a category upon mounts, a category upon their feet, and a category upon their faces." This is a censure, and it may be in the accusative (*manṣūb*) or the nominative (*marfū'*) case, or it may be a *mubtada'* (subject) whose *khabar* (predicate) is what follows. ﴿They are worse in position and further astray in way﴾. The one being compared to is the Messenger ﷺ, following the pattern of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that in recompense with Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He is angry﴾. It is as if it were said: what drives them to these questions is the belittling of his station and the misguiding of his path, while they do not know their own state, so that they might know that they are worse in position and further astray in way. It is also said that it is connected to His saying, ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in resting place﴾. The path is described as misguided by way of figurative attribution (*majaz 'aqli*) for emphasis.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 35–37:**

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book, and We appointed with him his brother Harun as a minister.﴾ He assisted him in the call (da'wah) and in raising the word (of Allah). That (his being a minister) does not contradict his sharing in prophethood, because those who share in a matter are the ones who assist one another in it.

﴿So We said: "Go, both of you, to the people who denied﴾ — meaning Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and his people — ﴿Our signs. Then We utterly destroyed them.﴾ That is, they both went to them, they denied the two of them, and so We destroyed them. He (Allah) limited the account to its two extremes, being satisfied with what is its intended purpose, namely the establishing of proof through the sending of messengers and the deserving of destruction through their denial. And the ordering (ta'qib, "then") is with regard to the ruling, not the actual occurrence. It is also read as "fa-dammartuhum" (فَدَمَّرْتُهم), "fa-dammaraahum" (فَدَمَّرَاهم), and "fa-dammaranna-hum" (فَدَمَّرانَّهم), with emphasis by the heavy nun (al-nun al-thaqilah).

﴿And the people of Nuh, when they denied the messengers﴾ — they denied Nuh and those before him, or Nuh alone; but the denial of one of the messengers is like the denial of all of them, or (it refers to) the sending of messengers in general, as with the Barahimah (Brahmins). ﴿We drowned them﴾ by the flood. ﴿And We made them﴾ — or We made their drowning or their story — ﴿a sign for mankind﴾, a lesson. ﴿And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.﴾ It may be general or specific; so it is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, to indicate their wrongdoing.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 38–39:

﴿And ʿĀd and Thamūd﴾ is conjoined either to "them" in (We made them) or to "the wrongdoers," because the meaning is "and We promised the wrongdoers." Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ read "wa-Thamūda" (without tanwīn), interpreting it as the tribe. ﴿And the companions of the Rass﴾: they were a people who worshipped idols, and Allah the Exalted sent to them Shuʿayb, but they denied him. While they were around the Rass, which is the unlined well, it collapsed, and they were swallowed up with their dwellings. It is also said that ﴿the Rass﴾ is a village in Falj al-Yamamah, in which there were remnants of Thamūd; a prophet was sent to them, but they killed him and so they perished. It is also said it is the Trench (al-Ukhdud), and it is also said it is a well at Antioch in which they killed Ḥabīb the carpenter. It is also said that they were the companions of Ḥanẓalah ibn Ṣafwān, the Prophet, whom Allah the Exalted tested with a great bird which had every color. They named it ʿAnqāʾ because of the length of its neck; it used to dwell on their mountain, which is called Fatkh or Damkh, and it would swoop down on their children and snatch them when hunting was scarce for it, and for this reason it was called "Mughrib" (the one that swoops). Ḥanẓalah invoked against it, and a thunderbolt struck it. Then they killed him, and so they were destroyed.

It is also said they were a people who denied their prophet and "rassū-hu," meaning they thrust him into a well. ﴿And generations﴾: and peoples of eras. It is said that a qarn is forty years, and it is said seventy, and it is said one hundred and twenty. ﴿Between that﴾: a reference to what has been mentioned. ﴿Many﴾: none knows them except Allah.

﴿And to each We presented the parables﴾: We made clear to him the wondrous stories from the stories of the former peoples, as warning and as establishing proof. When they persisted, they were destroyed, as He said: ﴿And to each We applied total destruction﴾: We crushed him into fragments. From it comes "tibr," the fragments of gold and silver. The first "kullan" is in the accusative governed by what is indicated by "ḍarabnā," like "andhharnā," and the second is governed by "tabbarnā," because it is unattached.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 40:**

﴿And they have certainly passed by﴾ — meaning the Quraysh, who passed many times in their trading journeys to al-Sham (Syria). ﴿the town which was rained upon with a rain of evil﴾ — meaning Sodom (Sadum), the greatest of the towns of the people of Lut (Lot), upon which stones were rained. ﴿Have they not then been seeing it?﴾ — during their repeated passages, so that they might take warning from what they saw in it of the traces of God's punishment. ﴿Rather, they did not expect a resurrection﴾ — rather, they were disbelievers who did not anticipate a resurrection or any consequence; therefore they did not reflect and did not take warning, so they passed by it as their mounts passed by. Or: they did not hope for a resurrection as the believers hope for it, longing for reward; or: they did not fear it, according to the Tihami dialect (al-lughah al-tihamiyyah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 41–42:

﴿When they see you, they take you only for mockery.﴾ They do not take you except as an object of ridicule or one who is mocked. ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The phrase is related after an implied saying, and the demonstrative (hadha, "this") expresses contempt. Placing ﴿God has sent as a messenger﴾ in the context of acknowledgment makes it a clause of their supposition, while at the height of denial, it is mockery and derision. Were it not for this, they would have said: "Is this the one who claims that God has sent him as a messenger?"

﴿Indeed he﴾ almost ﴿led us astray from our gods﴾ to divert us from their worship, through his excessive effort in calling to monotheism and the great number of proofs and miracles he presents for them, which come readily to mind. ﴿Had we not been steadfast in them﴾: we held firm and kept to their worship. The particle (lawla, "were it not") in such a construction restricts the absolute judgment in meaning, not in wording. ﴿They will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ This is like a response to their saying ﴿he almost led us astray﴾, for it indicates the negation of what it implies and is the cause of it. In it is a threat and an indication that He does not neglect them, even though He gives them respite.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 43–44:

﴿Have you seen him who takes his own desire as his god?﴾ That is, he obeys it and builds his religion upon it. He does not hear any proof, nor does he see any evidence. The second object (المفعول الثاني, al-maf'ul al-thani, the second object of the verb) was placed first for the sake of emphasis on it. ﴿Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ That is, a protector who keeps him from polytheism and sins while his condition is as it is. The first interrogation (الاستفهام, al-istifham, interrogation) is for confirmation (التقرير, al-taqrir) and wonder, and the second is for denial.

﴿Or do you think﴾ Rather, do you think? ﴿that most of them hear or understand?﴾ So that the verses or proofs would benefit them, and you would be concerned for their affair and hope for their faith. This is more blameworthy than what came before, so the turning away (الإضراب, al-idrab, a shift from one statement to another) was made to move from the former to this one. The specification of "most" is because among them were those who believed, and among them were those who understood the truth but were arrogant and obstinate out of pride and fear for their leadership. ﴿They are only like cattle﴾ in not benefiting from the verses striking their ears and in not reflecting on the signs and miracles they witnessed. ﴿Nay, they are even more astray in the way﴾ than cattle, because cattle submit to one who looks after them and distinguish one who does good to them from one who harms them, and they seek what benefits them and avoid what harms them. These people do not submit to their Lord, nor do they recognize His kindness from the harm of Satan, nor do they seek reward, which is the greatest benefit, nor do they guard against punishment, which is the greatest harm. Also, cattle, if they do not hold a true belief, do not acquire good, and so they hold no false belief and acquire no evil, unlike these people. Also, the ignorance of cattle harms no one, whereas the ignorance of these people leads to the stirring up of strife and the turning of people away from the truth. Also, cattle are not able to seek perfection, so there is no shortcoming on their part and no blame, whereas these people are deficient and deserve the greatest punishment for their shortcoming.

The first interrogation (الاستفهام, al-istifham, interrogation) is for confirmation (التقرير, al-taqrir) and wonder, and the second is for denial.

﴿Or do you think﴾ Rather, do you think? ﴿that most of them hear or understand?﴾ So that the verses or proofs would benefit them, and you would be concerned for their affair and hope for their faith. This is more blameworthy than what came before, so the turning away (الإضراب, al-idrab, a shift from one statement to another) was made to move from the former to this one. The specification of "most" is because among them were those who believed, and among them were those who understood the truth but were arrogant and obstinate out of pride and fear for their leadership. ﴿They are only like cattle﴾ in not benefiting from the verses striking their ears and in not reflecting on the signs and miracles they witnessed. ﴿Nay, they are even more astray in the way﴾ than cattle, because cattle submit to one who looks after them and distinguish one who does good to them from one who harms them, and they seek what benefits them and avoid what harms them. These people do not submit to their Lord, nor do they recognize His kindness from the harm of Satan, nor do they seek reward, which is the greatest benefit, nor do they guard against punishment, which is the greatest harm. Also, cattle, if they do not hold a true belief, do not acquire good, and so they hold no false belief and acquire no evil, unlike these people. Also, the ignorance of cattle harms no one, whereas the ignorance of these people leads to the stirring up of strife and the turning of people away from the truth. Also, cattle are not able to seek perfection, so there is no shortcoming on their part and no blame, whereas these people are deficient and deserve the greatest punishment for their shortcoming.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 45–46:

﴿Have you not considered your Lord﴾: Have you not looked at His handiwork? ﴿how He extended the shade﴾: how He spread it out. Or: Have you not looked at the shade, how your Lord extended it? He changed the arrangement (nazm, the construction of the phrase) to indicate that what is intended by this speech is the rational meaning, because its proof is clear. That proof is the indication of its having been brought into existence and its being directed in a beneficial manner through possible causes, and that this is the act of the Wise Maker, just as one witnesses what is seen. How much more so is this true of what is perceived by the senses from it. Or: Has your knowledge not reached the point that your Lord extended the shade between the rising of dawn and the sunrise, which is the most pleasant of states? Pure darkness repels the nature and blocks the sight, while the rays of the sun heat the air and dazzle the eye. For this reason He described Paradise with it, saying: "and shade extended" (56:30). ﴿And had He willed, He would have made it still﴾: fixed and stationary, from stillness (sukna), or not contracting from stillness, by making the sun remain in one position. ﴿Then We made the sun for it a guide﴾: for it does not become apparent to the senses until the sun rises, so that its light falls upon some of the bodies. Or: it is not found, nor does it vary, except through the sun's movement.

﴿Then We withdrew it to Us﴾: that is, We removed it by bringing the sun into its place. When He expressed its occurrences by "extension," in the sense of causing it to move, He expressed its removal by "withdrawal" to Himself, which carries the meaning of holding back. ﴿withdrawal, an easy withdrawal﴾: little by little, in proportion as the sun rises, so that the interests of the cosmos are ordered by this and countless benefits to creation are obtained. The "then" (thumma) in both places indicates the difference between matters, or the difference between the beginnings of the times of their appearance. It has been said: "He extended the shade" when He raised the heaven without a luminary and spread out the earth beneath it, so the earth cast its shadow upon it. And had He willed, He would have made it fixed in that state. Then He created the sun as a guide over it, that is, dominating it and following it, just as the proof follows what it proves; or as the guide of the road is the one who leads, for the shade varies by the movement of the sun and changes with its changing. ﴿Then We withdrew it to Us, an easy withdrawal﴾: gradually, until it reaches the limit of its diminishing. Or: an easy withdrawal at the establishment of the Hour, by withdrawing its causes, namely the bodies that cast shadow and that upon which shadow is cast.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 47:

﴿It is He who made the night for you as a garment﴾. He likened its darkness to a garment in its covering. ﴿And sleep as rest﴾: a repose for the bodies by cutting off their occupations. The root of sabat (rest, cessation) is qat' (cutting off), or [it means] death, as in His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you back to Himself at night﴾, because it severs life. From this comes al-masbut (the one who is struck with a deathlike sleep), said of the dead. ﴿And He made the day a resurrection﴾: meaning, possessing resurrection, i.e., dispersal (intishar), in which people spread out in search of livelihood. Or [it means] that one is raised from sleep in the manner of the raising of the dead, and so this is an indication that sleep and wakefulness are a model (unmudhaj) for death and resurrection. And from Luqman (peace be upon him): "O my son, just as you sleep and are awakened, so you die and are raised."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 48–49:

﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾. Ibn Kathir read it in the singular (rīḥ), intending the genus. (Nushran) means spreading out, scattering [the clouds] for the reckoning, plural of nashūr. Ibn 'Amir read it with a sukun (nushr) for lightness, and Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with that sukun and also with a fatha on the nun (nashr), as a verbal noun described by it. 'Asim read (bushran), the lighter form of bashsharа, plural of bashūr in the sense of mubashshir (one who gives good news), ﴿before His mercy﴾, that is, in front of the rain. ﴿And We send down from the sky pure water﴾, purifying, in accordance with His saying ﴿so that He may purify you thereby﴾. It is a noun for that by which one purifies, like the wuḍū' (ablution water) and the waqūd (fuel), for that with which one performs ablution and that with which one kindles a fire.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Dust is the purifier (ṭahūr) of the believer," and: "If a dog drinks from the vessel of one of you, it should be washed seven times, the first of them with dust."

It was also said that ṭahūr means eminent in purity. Fa'ūl, although it is predominantly used in both of these senses, has also come for the passive (maf'ūl), as in ḍabūth, for the verbal noun, as in qabūl, and for the noun, as in dhunūb. Describing water with it indicates the favour in it, and completes the blessing that follows, for pure water is more wholesome and more beneficial than that which is mixed with something that removes its purifying quality. It is also a reminder that if their outward parts are required to be purified, their inner parts are all the more deserving of it.

﴿That We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾, with vegetation. (Maytan) is in the masculine because (baldah) means (balad), and because it is not derived in the manner of the verbal forms, like the other intensive patterns, so it is treated as an inert noun.

﴿And We give drink from what We have created, to cattle and many humans﴾, meaning the people of the desert who live by rain. This is why cattle and humans are indefinite, and their specification is because the people of towns and villages live near rivers, and the benefits among them and the cattle around them are sufficient without rain. Other animals go far in search of water, so drink seldom fails them. Moreover, the context of these verses, as it is, is to demonstrate the greatness of power, so this is an enumeration of kinds of blessing. Cattle are a person's wealth, and most of their benefits and the chief of their livelihood depend on them. For this reason the watering of the cattle is mentioned before the watering of humans, just as the reviving of the land was mentioned before them, for it is the cause of their life and sustenance.

It was read as (nasqīhi) with a fatḥa, and saqā and asqā are two dialects. It was also said that asqāhu means he made a drink for him (saqyā). (Wa-anāsī) with the elision of a yā', is the plural of insī or insān, like ẓarābī for ẓarabān, with the original being anāsīn, and the nūn was changed to yā'.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 50:

﴿And indeed We have distributed it among them﴾ We have distributed this speech among people, in the Qur'an and the rest of the books; or [it refers to] the rain among them, in the different lands and the varying times and in the diverse forms, [such as] heavy rain, light drizzle and other [kinds]. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "No year is wetter than another, but Allah distributes that among His servants as He wills," and he recited this verse. Or [it refers to] among the rivers and the benefits.

﴿That they may take heed﴾ That they may reflect, know the perfection of power and the right of blessing in that, and rise to thank Him for it; or that they may take a lesson from the turning away of it from them and toward them. ﴿But most people refuse except ingratitude﴾ except the denial of the blessing and little concern for it; or its rejection, by saying, "We were given rain by such-and-such a star (nawʾ)." Whoever does not see rain except as coming from the stars (anwa') is a disbeliever, unlike one who sees that it is from the creation of Allah, while the stars are intermediaries and signs by His appointment, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 51–52:

﴿And had We willed, We would have sent a warner (nadhir) to every town.﴾ A prophet who would warn its people. He would thus lighten for you the burdens of prophethood. But We have restricted the matter to you, out of honour for you, magnifying your station, and preferring you over all the (other) Messengers. So meet that with steadfastness and diligence in the call and in manifesting the truth.

﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾ in what they want from you. This is an incitement (tahyij) to him, upon him be blessings and peace, and to the believers. ﴿And strive against them with it﴾ — with the Qur'an, or by refusing to obey them, which is indicated by "so do not obey." The meaning is that they strive to nullify your truth, so meet them (p-128)

with diligence in opposing them and in removing their falsehood. ﴿A great striving﴾ because striving against the foolish with proofs (hujaj) is greater than striving against enemies with the sword. Or because opposing and antagonizing them while they are among them, along with their arrogance (utuww) and dominance, is (greater). Or because it is a striving against all the disbelievers, since he was sent to all the towns.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 53:

﴿And it is He who let loose the two seas﴾, leaving them side by side, adjoining one another, such that they do not mix, from "maraja dabbatahu" (he let his beast loose to graze freely when he released it).

﴿This one is sweet and palatable﴾, quenching thirst by reason of its extreme sweetness. ﴿And this one is salty and bitter﴾, intensely briny. It is also read "milh" (with the vowel of a single noun), and its original form is probably "malih," which was lightened as in "bard" for "barid" (cold).

﴿And He placed between them a barrier﴾, a partition from His power. ﴿And an inviolable barrier﴾, and a complete repulsion, as though each of them says to the other what one who seeks refuge says to the one he seeks refuge from. It is also said: a fixed limit, like the Tigris that enters the sea and cleaves it, flowing through its midst for parasangs without its taste changing. It is also said that by the sweet sea is meant a great river such as the Nile, and by the salt sea the great ocean, and by the barrier the land that lies between them; so the power lies in the separation and the difference of attribute, even though the natural tendency of the parts of each element is to be joined, to adhere, and to be alike in quality.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 54–55:

﴿And He it is Who created man from water⁠—﴾ meaning: the One Who kneaded with it the clay of Adam. Or He made it a part of the substance of humankind, so that it would cohere, be pliable, and receive forms and shapes easily. Or [the water is] the sperm-drop (nutfah).

﴿Then He made him into lineage and marriage⁠—﴾ that is, He divided him into two kinds: those of lineage (nasab), namely males, to whom lineage is traced, and those of marriage (sihr), namely females, through whom marriage alliances are made. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He made of him the two spouses, the male and the female﴾.

﴿And your Lord is ever Competent⁠—﴾ in that He created from one substance a human being with diverse organs and widely differing natures, and made him into two opposite kinds. And He may create from a single drop twins, a male and a female.

﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which neither benefits them nor harms them⁠—﴾ meaning the idols, or everything that is worshipped besides Allah, since no created being has independent power to benefit or harm. ﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper [of Satan] against his Lord⁠—﴾ he backs Satan in enmity and in polytheism. By "the disbeliever" is meant either the category (jins) or Abu Jahl. It has also been said that the word ẓahīr means "despised, scorned," one whom He holds of no account, from the expression "you cast him behind your back" (ẓahharta bihi) when you discard him behind your back; so it is like His saying: ﴿Nor will Allah speak to them, nor look at them﴾.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 56–57:**

﴿We have sent you only as a bearer of good tidings and a warner.﴾ To the believers and the disbelievers.

﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it﴾ for conveying the message (tabligh, the delivery of the message), which is what is indicated by ﴿only as a bearer of good tidings and a warner﴾. ﴿except for whoever wills﴾ except the act of whoever wills ﴿to take a path to his Lord﴾: to draw near to Him and seek nearness to Him through faith and obedience. He expressed this in the form of a wage, since it is the intended purpose of the act, and made it an exception (istithna', exception) from it, to remove the suspicion of greed and to show the utmost compassion. In it, the Prophet's taking for himself, by exposing himself to reward and escaping punishment, is counted as a full and satisfying wage, restricted to him. It also indicates that their obedience returns to him as reward, insofar as it comes about through his guidance. It has also been said that the exception is disjunctive (munqati', disjunctive exception), meaning: "But whoever wills to take a path to his Lord, let him do so."(p-129)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 58–59:

﴿And rely upon the Living One who does not die﴾ in seeking protection from their evils and dispensing with their wages. For He is the one truly worthy of being relied upon, rather than the living ones who die, for when they die, whoever relied upon them is lost. ﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾: declare Him far above the attributes of deficiency, praising Him with the attributes of perfection, seeking an increase of favours through gratitude for His abundant bounties. ﴿And sufficient is He as one who is Aware of the sins of His servants﴾ of what appears of them and what is hidden. ﴿Aware﴾: One who is fully informed, so it is of no concern to you whether they believe or disbelieve.

﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne, the Most Merciful﴾. The discussion of this has already passed. Perhaps its mention is for further affirmation that He is truly worthy of being relied upon, inasmuch as He is the Creator of all and the One who disposes of it, and as an exhortation to steadfastness and deliberation in affairs, for He, may He be exalted, despite the completeness of His power and the swiftness of the execution of His command, created things in every case gradually and step by step. ﴿Al-Rahman﴾ is the predicate of ﴿alladhi﴾ if you make it the subject, and it is the predicate of an implied subject if you make it an attribute of ﴿al-Hayy﴾, or a substitute (badal) for the pronoun hidden in ﴿istawa﴾. It was also read in the genitive case as an attribute of ﴿al-Hayy﴾.

﴿Then ask about Him one who is aware﴾: ask about what has been mentioned of the creation and the establishing, one who is knowledgeable and will inform you of its reality, and that is Allah, the Exalted, or Jibril, or one who has found it in the earlier scriptures, so that he may confirm it for you. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to al-Rahman, and the meaning is: if they deny applying it to Allah, the Exalted, then ask about it those among the People of the Book who can inform you, so that they may recognise the occurrence of its synonym in their scriptures. On this basis, al-Rahman may be the subject, with the predicate being what follows it, and the question, just as it is transitive with ʿan because it implies the sense of inquiring, is transitive with bi (ب) because it implies the sense of concern. It has also been said that it is connected to ﴿khabiran﴾.

﴿Then ask about Him one who is aware﴾: ask about what has been mentioned of the creation and the establishing, one who is knowledgeable and will inform you of its reality, and that is Allah, the Exalted, or Jibril, or one who has found it in the earlier scriptures, so that he may confirm it for you. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to al-Rahman, and the meaning is: if they deny applying it to Allah, the Exalted, then ask about it those among the People of the Book who can inform you, so that they may recognise the occurrence of its synonym in their scriptures. On this basis, al-Rahman may be the subject, with the predicate being what follows it, and the question, just as it is transitive with ʿan because it implies the sense of inquiring, is transitive with bi (ب) because it implies the sense of concern. It has also been said that it is connected to ﴿khabiran﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 60–61:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to whatever you command us?" ﴾ Because they did not use this name (al-Rahman) for God, or because they thought that by it he meant something other than Him. For this reason they said: ﴿"Shall we prostrate to that which you command us?"﴾, i.e., to the one you command us, meaning, you command us to prostrate to him, or to your command to us without knowledge (irfan). It was also said that it was because it was a foreign word (mu'arrab) that they had not heard. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "ya'muruna" with the ya' (yā'), on the basis that it is the statement of some of them to others.

﴿And it increased them﴾, i.e., the command to prostrate to the Most Merciful, ﴿in aversion (nufur)﴾ from faith.

﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations (burujan)﴾, meaning the twelve constellations (al-buruj al-ithna 'ashara), which were named after this, and they are the lofty palaces, because they are for the wandering planets (al-kawakib al-sayyara) like dwellings for their inhabitants. Its derivation is from tabarruj (display), because of its visibility. ﴿And He placed in it a lamp (siraj)﴾, meaning the sun, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And He made the sun a lamp﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "surujan" (surujan), and these are the sun and the large stars. ﴿And a moon giving light (qamaran munira)﴾, shining at night. It was also read "wa-qamran" (qamran), i.e., possessing a moon, and it is the plural of qamra' (qamra'), and it is possible that it means the same as al-qumr, like al-rushd and al-rashad, al-'urb and al-'arab.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 62:

﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeed each other﴾ That is, [making them] possessors of succession (khilfah), each of the two replacing the other by taking its place in what a person ought to be doing in it, or by their alternating (yaʻtaqibani), in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the alternation of night and day﴾ [Qur'an 2:164]. The word khilfah is a noun of the state (lil-ḥālah) derived from khalafa, like rukbah (the manner of riding) and jilsah (the manner of sitting).

﴿for whoever wishes to be mindful﴾ by remembering the bounties of God and reflecting on His handiwork, so that he knows that there must be a Maker who is wise, self-existent (wājib al-dhāt), and merciful to His servants. ﴿Or wishes to be grateful﴾ by thanking God, exalted is He, for the blessings within it. Or [it means] that they are two times for those who remember and give thanks: whoever misses his portion of worship in one of them may make it up in the other. Ḥamzah recited ﴿an yadhdhakkara﴾ from dhakara with the meaning of tadhakkara, and likewise ﴿li-yadhdhakarū﴾; al-Kisa'i agreed with him in this.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 25, verses 63–64:

﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ is a *mubtada'* (subject) whose *khabar* (predicate) is ﴿those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber﴾. Or the predicate is ﴿those who walk upon the earth﴾. Their attribution to the Most Merciful is for specification and honour. Or it is because they are the most steadfast in His worship, on the reading that *'ibad* is the plural of *'abid* (worshipper), like *tajir* and *tujjar* (merchant and merchants).

﴿Humbly﴾: ﴿gently﴾, or ﴿a gentle walk﴾, where it is a *masdar* (verbal noun) used as a description. The meaning is that they walk with tranquillity and humility. ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾: meaning a parting greeting from you, and a leaving of you, with no good and no evil between us. Or it means ﴿a sound word﴾, by which they are safe from harm and sin. The verse of fighting does not contradict this, so as to abrogate it (*naskh*, abrogation), for what is meant is overlooking the foolish and not responding to them in speech.

﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾: in prayer. The spending of the night is singled out because worship at night is more arduous and further from showing off (*riya'*). The word *qiyaman* (standing) is placed later for the sake of the rhyme (*ruwiyy*). It is the plural of *qa'im* (one who stands), or a *masdar* treated as such.

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever-clinging."﴾ *Gharaman* means constant and inescapable, and from the same root comes *al-gharim* (the debtor), because he is held to his debt. This indicates that they, despite their good dealings with people and their diligence in worshipping the Truth, fear the punishment and earnestly beseech Allah Most High to avert it from them, because they do not take pride in their deeds and are not confident that their states will continue.

﴿Indeed it is wretched as a dwelling-place and a station.﴾ That is, *bi'sat mustaqarran* (it is wretched as a place of settlement). Here there is an ambiguous pronoun (*damir mubham*), which is explained by the specification (*tamyiz*) and by the noun of blame (*al-makhsus bil-dhamm*), and there is a deleted pronoun through which the sentence is connected to the subject of *inna*. Alternatively, the verb is *ahzanat* (it has caused grief), in which case the pronoun is the noun of *inna*, and *mustaqarran* is either a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) or a specification (*tamyiz*). The sentence then serves as a causal explanation of the first reason, or as a second reason. Both readings allow that the words are reported speech (*hikaya*) or that they originate from Allah Himself.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 67:

﴿And those who, when they spend, neither act extravagantly nor are niggardly﴾ — they do not go beyond the limit of generosity (karam), "and neither are they stingy" — they do not constrict in the manner of the miser (shahih).

It is said: extravagance (al-israf) is spending on what is forbidden (al-maharim), and constriction (al-taqtir) is withholding what is obligatory (al-wajib). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read yuqtiru with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ta' (yaqturu, from qatara). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ta' (yuqtiru, from aqtara). It was also read with tashdid (shaddah), and all of these amount to the same meaning. ﴿And that is ever between that a standard﴾ — (qawaman) meaning a middle course, just and balanced; it was so named because both extremes are straight, just as "sawa'" (equal) was so named because both sides are level. It was also read with a kasra (qiwaman), which is that by which needs are met, neither exceeding nor falling short of them. The word is either a second predicate (khabar thani) or an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal muakkidah). It is also permissible for the predicate to be "bayna dhalika" as an adverbial complement (laghwan). It has also been said that qawaman is the subject of kana, but it is indeclinable (mabni) because it is attached to a non-declinable element; this view is weak, because it means "al-qawam," so it would be like informing about a thing by means of itself.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 68–69:

﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾ — i.e., He has forbidden it, in the sense that He has forbidden its killing. ﴿Except by right﴾ — this is connected to the omitted verb "killing," or to "do not kill." ﴿Nor do they commit fornication﴾ — after affirming for them the foundations of obedience, He negates for them the chief of sins, to show the perfection of their faith, to indicate that the mentioned reward is promised to one who combines all of that, and to allude to the disbelievers by their opposites. For this reason He follows it with a threat, warning them, so He said: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ — as a recompense for sin (āthām), or "sin" (ithman) with an implied recompense. It is also read as "ayyāman," meaning hardships; one says "a day full of ayyām," i.e., a difficult day.

﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection﴾ — a substitute (badal) for ﴿yalqa﴾, because it has the same meaning, like his saying:

"Whenever you visit us and descend upon our abodes, you will find firewood, thick and blazing fire."

Abu Bakr read it with the nominative (raf'), as a resumption (istinaf) or as a circumstantial clause (hal); and likewise ﴿and he will abide therein in humiliation﴾. Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read "yuḍaʻʻif" with the jussive (jazm), and Ibn 'Amir with the nominative in both, with the doubling and the omission of the alif in "yuḍaʻʻif." It is also read "wa-yukhlad" in the passive, lightened, and it is read heavy. The doubling of the punishment means its multiplication, because sin is combined with disbelief, and his saying indicates this:

Or: he turns repentance back to Allah, who loves those who repent and treats them with favour. Or: he returns to Allah and to His reward with a good return. This is a generalization after a specification.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 72–73:

﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood﴾: they do not establish false testimony, or they do not attend gatherings of falsehood, for being present at falsehood is a form of participation in it. ﴿And when they pass by idle talk﴾: that which ought to be cast aside and discarded. ﴿They pass by with dignity﴾: turning away from it, honouring themselves by refraining from stopping at it and plunging into it. Among this is overlooking indecencies, pardoning sins, and using euphemism for what is shameful to state explicitly.

﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord﴾: by admonition or by recitation. ﴿They do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾: they do not stand over them without being attentive to them or seeing what is in them, like one who neither hears nor sees; rather, they bend over them, hearing with attentive ears and looking with watchful eyes. So the negation here is of the state, not of the act, as when you say: "Zayd does not meet me greeting me" (lā yalqānī Zaydun musallliman). It has also been said that the pronoun (hā', in "ʿalayhā") refers to the sins implied by (bi-l-laghw) ["idle talk"].

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 74:

﴿And those who say: "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring the coolness of our eyes"﴾ — by their being granted success in obedience and in attaining virtues. For when a believer's family join him in the obedience of God, his heart is gladdened by them and his eye is cooled by them, because he sees them assisting him in the religion and anticipates their joining him in Paradise. The particle "min" (min) here is either for the beginning of the source (ibtida'iyyah) or explanatory (bayaniyyah), as in your saying: "I saw from you a lion." Hamzah, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read «wa-dhurriyyatina» (in the singular), while Ibn 'Amir, the two men of Mecca and Medina, Hafs and Ya'qub read ﴿wa-dhurriyyatina﴾ with the alif (in the plural). The indefiniteness of "a'yun" (a'yun, "eyes") is to indicate the indefiniteness of "qurrah" (qurrah, "coolness"), for magnification and for lessening it, since what is meant is the eyes of the God-fearing, and these are few in comparison with the eyes of others. ﴿And make us a leader (imam) for the God-fearing﴾ — they will follow us in matters of religion, through the addition of knowledge and success in action. Its being singular is either to indicate the genus and to avoid ambiguity, as in His saying ﴿Then He brings you forth as a child﴾, or because it is a verbal noun (masdar) in origin, or because what is meant is "make each one of us (a leader)," or because they are like a single soul in the unity of their path and the agreement of their word. It has also been said that it is the plural of "amm" (amm, one who intends), like "sa'im" and "siyam," and its meaning is: intending them, following them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 75–76:

﴿They are the ones who will be rewarded with the ghurfah (the high chambers)﴾, the highest places of Paradise. It is a collective noun (ism jins) intended to denote the plural, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will be secure in the chambers (al-ghurufat)﴾. It is also read with the plural form. It is said that it is one of the names of Paradise. ﴿For what they endured﴾: for their patience over hardships, from the bitterness of acts of obedience, the renunciation of desires, and the bearing of struggles. ﴿And they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾: a supplication for long life and safety, meaning the angels will greet them and salute them. Or, one of them will greet the other and salute him. Or, it means lasting continuity and safety from every calamity. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read (yalqawna) from laqiya (to meet).

﴿Abiding therein﴾: they will not die therein nor will they leave. ﴿How good it is as a place of rest and abode﴾: it is the counterpart of ﴿evil it is as a place of rest﴾ in meaning, and similar to it in its grammatical construction (i'rab).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 77:

﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you, were it not for your supplication."﴾ It means: "What would my Lord do with you?", from *ʿabbaʾtu al-jaysh* (I arranged the army) when I prepared it. Or it means: "He would not count you of any worth." ﴿Were it not for your supplication﴾ means: were it not for your worship. The honour and dignity of a human being lie in knowledge (*maʿrifa*) and obedience (*ṭāʿa*). Otherwise, he is equal to the rest of the animals. It has also been said that the meaning is: "What would my Lord do with your punishment, were it not for your calling upon Him along with other gods?" If *mā* is interrogative, then its position is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), as if it were said: "What kind of concern would He have for you?"

﴿Then you have denied﴾ what I informed you of, in that you opposed it. It has also been said: "Then you have fallen short in worship," from the expression *kadhaba al-qitāl* (the fighting was lax), when one does not exert oneself in it. It has been recited as "Then the disbelievers have denied" (*fa-qad kadhaba al-kāfirūn*), meaning the disbelievers among you. This is because the address is directed to people in general, with what exists in their kind of worship and denial.

﴿So it will be inevitable﴾ means the consequence of denial will be inescapable, befalling you without doubt. Or its effect will be inescapable for you, until it throws you face down into the Fire. The subject was left unexpressed without mention for the sake of awe and warning, and to indicate that no description can encompass it. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the killing on the Day of Badr, and that they were bound together among the slain, *lizāman*. It has been recited as *lazāman* with a fatḥa, meaning "the state of being bound," like *al-thabāt* and *al-thubūt* (steadfastness and firmness).

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Furqan will meet Allah while he is a believer that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it, and he will be admitted into Paradise without hardship."
